entries.title: CPS wins back millions in federal funding after Trump administration settles lawsuit
entries.summary: <p>Chicago Public Schools has won back millions of dollars in federal grants that top education officials took away after concluding that the school district had violated students’ civil rights by having a Black Student Success Plan and policies that support transgender students.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://clearinghouse.net/case/47906/" target="_blank" ><u>CPS sued the federal government in March</u></a> alleging that the grants were taken away without following the process required by law. That case was settled on Thursday after the U.S. Department of Education agreed to return the funds by Friday, according to a court document dismissing the case.</p><p>CPS officials did not say how much money they expected to be released as part of the settlement. But when the Education Department announced last year that it was stripping the grant, it said it would withhold about $6 million, as well as funding for future years.</p><p>“The District looks forward to working with the U.S. Department of Education to ensure these resources reach schools and students as quickly as possible,” a CPS spokesperson wrote in an email Friday.</p><p>Though it’s a relatively small amount compared to CPS’ $10 billion budget, the settlement reverses the most tangible action taken by the Trump administration against CPS. It is one of several efforts by the Trump administration to force school districts to roll back civil rights and Title IX protections against sex-based discrimination, especially as they pertain to transgender students.</p><p>The Education Department did not respond to questions about why it settled the case.</p><p>CPS officials and board members have refused to back down from their policies, though they have tried not to pick a public fight over them. CPS did not publicly announce that it was suing the federal government or that the case was settled, a fact that was <a class="Link" href="https://news.bloomberglaw.com/litigation/education-department-settles-suit-over-chicago-school-grant-cuts" target="_blank" ><u>first reported by Bloomberg Law</u></a>.</p><p>Since Trump returned to office in 2025, the Education Department and Congress have launched multiple investigations and reviews of CPS policies and spending. As recently as this week, the Republican-led U.S. House Committee on Education and the Workforce <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/08/27/house-education-committee-reviewing-whether-cps-policies-that-support-transgender-students-violate-federal-law" target="_blank" ><u>demanded that CPS send policies and complaints</u></a> as the committee continues to review whether CPS’ protections for transgender students should prompt changes to federal law.</p><p>Education Department officials contend that having a plan that endeavors to improve academic outcomes for Black students harms white and Asian students and educators.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/09/17/feds-threaten-cps-magnet-school-grants-over-black-student-success-plan-treatment-of-trans-students" target="_blank" ><u>In a 2025 letter to CPS</u></a>, Craig Trainor, the acting assistant secretary for civil rights at the time, called the plan “textbook racial discrimination.” He went on to say “no justification proffered by CPS can overcome the patent illegality of its racially exclusionary plan.”</p><p>In that letter, he demanded that CPS abolish the plan.</p><p>He also attacked CPS policies that allow transgender students to play sports and use locker rooms and restrooms that correspond with their gender identity. Trainor wrote in the 2025 letter that those policies are “facially discriminatory on the basis of sex.”</p><p>In CPS’ lawsuit over the loss of the grant, the district contends that it has fully cooperated with the Office for Civil Rights’ investigation into these policies. Yet despite its compliance and the fact that reviews of these policies went away, the Education Department took away the grant.</p><p>The grants are to support some of CPS’ specialized magnet programs. In the lawsuit, CPS points out that the grant specifically went to personalized learning programs and science, engineering and technology classes in high-need schools.</p><p>Without the federal money, CPS had to find other money to cover staff salaries and use contingency funding to continue after-school programs. The “abrupt discontinuation” of the grants “without notice, hearing opportunity or any semblance of due process, significantly undermines the work that CPS engaged in for over 10 years in developing high quality programs,” the lawsuit states.</p><p>CPS officials said they planned to use the returned grant funding “to support continued, high-quality magnet school programming,” though the amount that will be available for this school year is still being determined.</p>

entries.title: Suburban Cook County reports first 4 West Nile virus cases of 2026
entries.summary: <p>The Cook County Department of Public Health has reported the first four cases of West Nile virus in suburban Cook County this year and is urging residents to take precautions against mosquito bites.</p><p>All four cases were identified in adults, the health department said Friday.</p><p>Dr. Kiran Joshi, chief operating officer of Cook County Department of Public Health, urged residents to take steps to protect themselves from mosquitoes.</p><p>“Using insect repellent, wearing long sleeves and pants, and eliminating standing water around your home can help protect you from mosquito bites,” Joshi said in a news release.</p><p>West Nile virus occurs in humans when they are bitten by mosquitoes that contracted the virus from infected birds.</p><p>As of the week ending Aug. 22, the risk of human West Nile virus infection is considered high, the department said.</p><h3>West Nile virus in Illinois</h3><p>The Illinois Department of Public Health on Wednesday reported the state’s first human case of West Nile virus in Piatt County.</p><p>Mosquitoes carrying the virus were <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/06/12/first-west-nile-virus-cases-of-the-year-reported-in-mosquitoes-in-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>reported</u></a> in Illinois in May, but no human cases had been reported at the time.</p><p>Suburban Cook County reported  four deaths related to the virus in 2025, with 44 total cases reported last year, according to the department.</p><p>Instances of West Nile virus increased significantly in 2025 across Illinois compared to 2024, according to the department.</p><p>The state reported 150 confirmed human cases of the virus in 2025, more than doubling the 69 cases reported in 2024. Ten deaths were reported in 2025, compared with 13 deaths the year before. </p><p>Health officials warned that many people infected with West Nile virus have no symptoms and do not become ill. </p><p>Some may develop mild symptoms like fever, headache, rash, and body aches within three to 15 days after infection.</p><p>More severe symptoms can be neuroinvasive, impacting the nervous system, the brain or spinal cord. These symptoms can include high fever, stiff neck, confusion, muscle weakness, and inflammation of the brain, which can cause permanent neurological damage or death. </p><p>In June, CCDPH launched its annual “Fight the Bite” public awareness campaign to encourage residents to take precautions against West Nile virus.</p><h3>How to prevent West Nile virus infection</h3><p>The campaign encourages simple steps to reduce the risk of West Nile virus infection.</p><p>People are encouraged to use EPA-registered insect repellents to ward off the bugs.</p><p>Adults should use repellents containing 20% to 50% DEET, the department said. Child-friendly repellents containing 20% to 30% DEET are recommended for children. </p><p>Residents should also eliminate standing water from flowerpots, old tires, buckets, birdbaths and plastic wading pools where mosquitoes can breed.</p><p>Damaged windows and door screens can also let mosquitoes in. The health department urged people to check that their door and window screens fit tightly and do not have holes or gaps to protect indoor spaces.</p><p> Residents are also reminded to take caution and consider limiting outdoor activities at dawn and dusk when possible as mosquito activity is heightened during these hours. </p><p>To learn more about West Nile virus prevention, visit <a class="Link" href="http://fightthebitecookcounty.com" target="_blank" ><u>FightTheBiteCookCounty.com</u></a>.</p>

entries.title: Davis Martin eyes return to rotation, and first-half form, for home stretch of White Sox’ playoff push
entries.summary: <p>MINNEAPOLIS — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> starter Davis Martin was relegated to watching his teammates from afar while nursing a blister on the middle finger that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/14/white-sox-put-davis-martin-on-injured-list-call-up-jose-urquidy" target="_blank" ><u>has sidelined him</u></a> for two weeks.</p><p>Suffice to say he’s happy to be watching from the dugout this weekend in Minneapolis, and he’ll be thrilled to be back on the mound next week in Houston.</p><p>“It's huge,” Martin said after rejoining the team Friday following a quick, sharp Triple-A rehab assignment. “I told my wife after just one day in Charlotte, I was just like, ‘I miss my guys. I'm seeing [Tristan Peters] hit <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/26/tristan-peters-white-sox-munetaka-murakami-colson-montgomery-franchise-record-frank-thomas-paul-konerko-carlos-lee-will-venable" target="_blank" ><u>his fifth home run</u></a>.’ I had, like, the super FOMO as I was sitting in my hotel room by myself in Charlotte. I miss my guys, I miss my team, I miss all that. I just want to be back.”</p><p>With a pitching staff gasping toward the finish line in the heat of a pennant race, the Sox are missing Martin just as much — especially the version of Martin they got over the first few months of the season, when their longest-tenured player’s breakout put him in All-Star consideration.</p><p>But it’s been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/04/davis-martin-chicago-white-sox-boston-red-sox-joey-bart-caleb-durbin-edgar-quero-roch-cholowsky" target="_blank" ><u>a slog since late June</u></a> for Martin, whose ERA ballooned to 4.32 before the blister did on his throwing hand.</p><p>At this stage, the Sox will take just about anything they can get from Martin, a week removed from their last game with anyone in the rotation clearing five innings and flagging reliability in starters not named Sean Burke or <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/19/white-sox-rotation-anthony-kay-davis-martin-erick-fedde-will-venable-noah-schultz-jose-urquidy-kyle-teel-zach-bove-cameron-johnson" target="_blank" ><u>Anthony Kay</u></a>.</p><p>The need was made all the more apparent early in the Sox' series opener at Target Field, where the Twins roughed up trade-deadline acquisition Luis Castillo for four runs on seven hits over the first three innings. Sox hitters have done their part to pick up the slack. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Colson Montgomery sent that one outta here! 🚀 <a href="https://t.co/h7gcDIT2Hb">pic.twitter.com/h7gcDIT2Hb</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://x.com/whitesox/status/2093495551333474607?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 29, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Martin evoked his first-half form with five innings of scoreless, one-hit ball on Thursday for the Knights, walking one and fanning five while throwing 40 of his 59 pitches for strikes.</p><p>The 29-year-old right-hander often looked unhittable over the first two-plus months of the season, but has labored to a 6.52 ERA over his last 15 starts. His IL stint was as valuable for physical recovery as it was mental.</p><p>“It was a good time to mentally reset,” he said. “Good time to really just focus in on bullpens, be able to actually get stuff out of bullpens because you are fresher than just your normal Day Two ‘pen after throwing 100 pitches so you're able to work on stuff, you're able to really dive into a lot of these things, and I think we did a really good job of refining all that stuff, and I think mentally, we're in a really good spot.”</p><p>With Martin lined up to start Tuesday but not yet officially penciled in, manager Will Venable called it “really important to get him back and healthy and [to] kind of stabilize our rotation.”</p><p>“He's been one of our guys in the middle of everything all year,” Venable said. “Obviously, we know that when he's right, what he's capable of doing, he's been as valuable as any player. So to have him back, and get that type of player back, that guy that's a leader in our clubhouse in every way possible — he makes an impact on our club.”</p><p>The timing is not lost on Venable, whose squad has four more key division series over the final month of the season.</p><p>“They're going to decide it all,” the second-year manager said. “It’s what it's all about, being able to take care of your own division. And in our case, every one of these clubs in our division are really good.”</p><p>And Martin wouldn’t miss it for the world.</p><p>“It's everything that we worked for,” he said. “We had a few team meetings last year basically saying, ‘Hey, if you don't believe that we can do this, like, you don't need to be in this room.’ And a lot of guys that were on that team are still here and still ready to roll and still pushing… Now it's just time to finish. It's time to empty the tank and give it everything we got.”</p>
entries.author: Mitchell Armentrout
